title: Graduation Photo Poses For the Proud Newly Grads
summary: Graduation poses for cap-and-gown photos: what to do with your hands, your diploma and your tassel, plus poses that work in a crowd.
body_markdown:
## Four years, one afternoon, forty photos


You will wear this gown for about three hours. Somewhere inside them, someone will say "let's get some photos" and point a camera at you on a lawn full of families doing exactly the same thing.


Here is what nobody mentions. Every pose you default to relies on something the gown takes away. Hands in pockets: there are no pockets. Arms relaxed at your sides: the sleeves swallow them. Weight on one hip: the fabric hangs straight and hides it. Your usual repertoire is gone, which is why so many graduation photos end up as a person standing square to the lens holding a rolled tube of paper.


The fix is not more poses. It is three that work with the gown, plus a plan for who you shoot with and in what order.


## Why a gown breaks the poses you already know


A gown is a rectangle. It removes your waist, hides your hips and turns your arms into two dark shapes hanging off a dark shape. Stand square to the camera and the frame flattens into a silhouette with a face on top.


Two adjustments solve most of it. Turn your body about forty-five degrees away from the camera and bring your face back toward it, which gives the gown a front edge and a side. Then get one arm away from your body: bend an elbow, hold the cap, put a hand on a railing. Any gap between arm and torso is light getting through, and light is what separates you from the fabric.


The cap has its own rule. Wear it flat and level rather than tipped back, and turn your head slightly toward the tassel side so the tassel sits against your cheek.


## Solo poses that work in cap and gown


Start walking. Ask whoever is shooting to catch the walk toward them and the walk away, and to keep shooting through both. Your shoulders drop when you move and your face stops performing.


Then sit down. Steps are the best furniture on any campus. One knee up, the other leg extended, forearms resting on the raised knee. Seated poses solve the arm problem outright because your hands now have a job.


For the diploma, hold it low and angled across your body rather than up at chest height like a trophy. High and centred blocks your torso and shortens your neck. If you have the certificate rather than the tube, hold it open and look down at it for one frame. That one tends to be the print.


Save the cap throw for last and do it at least six times. The frame where your face is visible and the cap is still in the air is the rarest thing in graduation photography.


## Poses with the people who got you there


Give the parents the photo they have always wanted first, so it is done. Then do the better ones: have both parents turn in toward you rather than facing forward, and get one of just you and whoever cried.


Friends already know how to stand near each other. Two arrangements are worth planning: a staggered line, where you alternate who steps half a pace forward so the group has depth, and a group toss on a shared count. Shoot the toss from slightly low so the caps clear the roofline.


## Where to shoot, and what the weather will do


Shoot the crowded landmark first, before the lawn fills up. Move to quieter architecture second, and finish somewhere green and open. Two or three locations is plenty.


Our guide to[five things that make graduation photos work](https://www.snappr.com/blog/5-great-tips-for-perfect-graduation-photos) covers the planning side, and the city spot guides are worth ten minutes first. There are lists for[graduation photography in Los Angeles](https://www.snappr.com/blog/top-5-spots-for-graduation-photography-in-los-angeles) and[graduation photos in Brisbane](https://www.snappr.com/blog/top-5-spots-for-graduation-photos-in-brisbane) .


Two conditions matter. Put any breeze behind you or across you, never into your front, where it presses the gown flat. And keep the sun behind or beside you rather than in front, since a gown over clothes plus a squint is the standard bad graduation frame.


## Book a graduation shoot


The window is short and the light is only good for part of it, which is the argument for having someone there whose one job is the photographs. ## Frequently asked questions


### What should I do with my hands in graduation photos?


Give them a job: hold your cap, hold the diploma low and angled across your body, or rest a forearm on a raised knee when seated. The goal is a visible gap between arm and torso, which is what stops the gown reading as a flat shape.


### Should I hold my diploma open or closed?


Do both. Hold the tube low and angled for standing frames, then take one looking down at the open certificate. The looking-down frame is quieter than the trophy pose and tends to be the one people print.


### When should graduation photos be taken, before or after the ceremony?


Before, if the schedule allows. Hair is fresh, the gown is uncreased and the lawn is emptier. If it has to be after, go straight to your locations before anyone changes clothes.


### What poses work for group graduation photos?


Stagger the line so half the group steps forward a pace, which gives the frame depth instead of a flat row. For a cap toss, count out loud and shoot from slightly below so the caps clear the buildings. Keep groups under about eight people so faces stay readable.
